title: Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp.
summary: The courts enforced specific written disclaimers of reliance on statements about the film and its participants, defeating the pleaded fraud challenges to the Borat releases.
notes: The sample Borat release reproduced at Supplement pages 35–36 arose in another participant lawsuit, according to its editorial note. It illustrates the form; it should not be represented as the exact signed document of every plaintiff in this case. The appellate ruling is identified in the supplement as a summary order not selected for publication in the Federal Reporter.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were driving instructor Michael Psenicska, etiquette-business owner Cindy Streit and dinner guests, and etiquette instructor Kathie Martin. They sued the film’s producers and associated defendants for claims arising from their appearances in Borat.
sections.Material Facts:
Psenicska alleged that a producer described an educational documentary about foreigners adapting to American life. The crew arrived ninety minutes late with $500 and a release; he signed without reading because he lacked his reading glasses and was concerned about another appointment. Streit arranged a filmed dinner after representations about a Belarusian dignitary and television documentary. Her guests signed shortly before filming. Martin received $350 and signed a standard release before the filmed etiquette session. Each later objected to offensive behavior, the film’s actual character, or the portrayal of the participants.

The agreements authorized a documentary-style film intended to entertain a young-adult audience and released a broad range of claims, including fraud and privacy claims. More specifically, paragraph 5 disclaimed reliance on promises or statements concerning the film’s nature and the identity of its participants or makers. That subject-specific disclaimer, rather than an undifferentiated entire-agreement clause alone, drove the fraud analysis.
sections.Procedural History: The Southern District of New York granted Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal of the three actions in 2008, considering the agreements incorporated into the complaints. The Second Circuit affirmed in a 2009 summary order reproduced immediately after the district-court opinion. Both courts evaluated the legal effect of the writings while accepting the properly pleaded factual allegations for purposes of dismissal.
sections.Issue: Was “documentary-style” ambiguous as applied to Borat, and could alleged false oral descriptions invalidate the releases despite the express disclaimer of reliance on those subjects?
sections.Holding: The relevant language was unambiguous, Borat fell within its documentary-style description, and the specific reliance disclaimer defeated the alleged fraudulent-inducement claims under the New York law applied. The dismissals were affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The courts distinguished a film’s style from a guarantee that its protagonist and narrative were entirely genuine. Real interviews and events presented as the travels of a fictional character still fit the agreed documentary-style description. A disagreement about whether the plaintiffs liked that use did not establish a second reasonable meaning of the contract.

Fraudulent inducement required reasonable reliance. Applying Danann, the courts reasoned that plaintiffs could not establish reliance on oral representations about precisely the subjects as to which they had expressly disclaimed reliance. The appellate court also considered the exception for facts peculiarly within the other party’s knowledge. It found that plaintiffs could have requested written assurances on a deal-breaking issue or walked away without collateral harm. On the allegations presented, recasting the asserted misrepresentations as nondisclosure did not avoid the same reliance problem. The decision does not approve deception as desirable conduct or announce that every general merger clause defeats fraud.

textbookImport.basis: Paraphrase of the exact supplied Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement; no subsequent-treatment review.

learning.why: This case links fraud, interpretation, signed releases, and assent. Its result depends on the disclaimer’s specificity and the courts’ account of available precautions.

topics.assent: Examines the effect of signing a release that disclaims reliance on particular oral representations.
topics.misrepresentation: Specific reliance disclaimers defeat the fraud theories on this record.
topics.interpretation: Distinguishes documentary style from a promise of a wholly factual documentary.
topics.parol-evidence: Illustrates why a specific no-reliance clause matters beyond a general integration clause.
topics.standard-forms: Tests enforcement of broad releases in a standardized consent form.
